Photograph: Tyrone Siu/Reuters Arms trade Australia investigating how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for US went missing in Hong Kong Disappearance of jet components sparks concern some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Sarah Basford Canales Tue 22 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT First published on Tue 22 Sep 2026 03.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Department of Defence is examining how F-35 fighter jet parts bound for the US from Australia were unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, the acting prime minister, Richard Marles , has said. Marles said “very much everything that has occurred at the Australian end” would be reviewed, but claimed the technology parts were not “sensitive”, as first reported by Politico over the weekend . The parts, which were being transported by another unknown third party on behalf of manufacturer, Lockheed Martin, still remain unaccounted for months later following their unplanned diversion to Hong Kong . The last known location of the fighter jet components – in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China – has sparked concern that some of the program’s technology secrets could have been exposed. “We are examining [Australia’s involvement], but the point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the program, and through the US’s prime contractor, Lockheed,” Marles said on Tuesday. “My understanding is that there is a sense of comfort, and we’re not talking about sensitive equipment here, or sensitive parts. View image in fullscreen A Royal Australian Air Force F-35 flying over New South Wales. Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAP “Ultimately, though, this is an issue which is going to be managed by the United States and by Lockheed in terms of what has occurred.” Politico reported sources said the “sensitive” shipment contained one of the jet’s canopies, which reportedly contains stealth technology. The US Department of War and F-35 Joint Program Office confirmed they were aware of the “shipment issue”. “We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident, and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence,” the spokesperson said. While many details have not yet been revealed, Michael Shoebridge, a director for Strategic Analysis Australia who has worked in intelligence agencies, said there were two reasons why China, or another adversary, would want F-35 parts – to reverse engineer them, or to learn how to better exploit and attack them. Shoebridge added the shipment’s pitstop in Hong Kong was “such an unexpectedly stupid thing” for the manufacturer or Australia to do. “This is an act of incredible ineptitude and stupidity, and so it’s more the Chinese taking advantage of an incredible stroke of luck brought to them by the stupidity of the people involved,” he said. Last week, the US State Department announced that the Trump administration would continue with the sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia, despite reported concerns from the US intelligence organisations that China could obtain some of the stealth technology. Australia was one of the early development partners in the F-35. The program spreads the development, supply, management and sustainment of the fighter jets across different countries. More than 70 Australian companies have production and sustainment contracts with the F-35 program. In excess of 700 of the fighter jet’s “critical pieces” are manufactured in Victoria alone , according to the state government. Australia also hosts a regional distribution hub for F-35 parts in New South Wales. Australian companies involved in the program’s supply chain have been awarded contracts valued at over $5.2bn, as of September 2025. Shoebridge said the missing shipment of parts could mean the whole multibillion-dollar fleet is vulnerable to adversaries. “They’re all now carrying the risk of whatever vulnerabilities this has brought to the aircraft,” he said. “So it’s not just a US-Australia issue. It’s every operator of the F-35 program [that] has an interest in understanding what happened and what was potentially exposed.” Explore more on these topics Arms trade Australian foreign policy US military Australian politics Hong Kong Asia Pacific Richard Marles news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/22/over.text: Russia and Ukraine traded attacks overnight, with seven killed on the Ukrainian side, authorities said on Thursday, despite renewed diplomatic efforts involving the United States.The attacks came shortly after US envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian president Vladimir Putin in Saint Petersburg for talks on ending the war.In Ukraine, authorities say those killed include a man in Sumy, a woman in Kharkiv, three people in Zaporizhzhia and two in Donetsk.In the capital, Kyiv, the mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on social media that strikes had wounded 15 people in the capital, eight of whom had been taken to hospital.In another post that strikes had damaged metro infrastructure at the Pivdenny Bridge, which officials said had restricted traffic between parts of the city.Ukraine's Airforce had posted warnings on Telegram throughout the early hours of "ballistic missiles towards Kyiv" and reports of fighter jets, and instructed residents to stay in shelters.On Thursday morning, the airforce said it had shot down an 181 Russian UAVs overnight, adding there were still strike drones in the air.In Russia, the mayor of Moscow Sergei Sobyanin said that two people had been wounded during mostly-intercepted barrages of 630 drones headed towards the region, 163 of which were approaching the capital city. Elsewhere, the governor of Tula said air defences destroyed 70 drones, while Lipetsk’s governor reported one man wounded.US talks with RussiaPresident Donald Trump said following the meeting with Putin and Witkoff, the two sides were “maybe now the closest we’ve been” to ending the conflict, although no breakthrough was announced.The Kremlin said it was “in principle” willing to resume trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US, potentially in mid-November after the US midterm elections.Ukraine has also backed renewed trilateral negotiations, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying Kyiv wanted a meeting as soon as possible.Witkoff described his talks with Putin as “constructive”, while acknowledging that “important work” remained.Following the talks, Russia agreed to release US citizen Stephen Hubbard, a retired teacher convicted by Russia of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine, allegations he has denied.Trump has delayed further sanctions on Russia, saying doing so had helped secure Hubbard’s release.Trump also struck a fresh agreement with Russia to sell diesel, aimed at reducing fuel prices that have risen during the wider Middle East conflict, a move that has drawn criticism from Kyiv and several European governments.
